## Loading necessary libraries for this assignment:

```{r libraries}

library(p8105.datasets) # To load our data
library(tidyverse) # For pipes and ggplot
library(hexbin) # Using for Problem 1 plot
library(patchwork) # For visualization
library(ggridges) # For visualization

```

## Problem 1: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Data Set

Our problem utilizes data from the NY National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) data.To start, we will load and explore the data. Per the instructions, our data is obtained from our course's _p8105.datasets_ package, loaded above. We can then use the _head()_, _nrow()_, and _ncol()_ functions to explore our variables:

```{r loading_exploring}

# Loading the NOAA data:

data("ny_noaa")

# Exploring our data set:

head(ny_noaa) # Obtaining the names of the variables in the data set
str(ny_noaa) # Obtaining the data types of each variable

# We can also look at the extent of NA values in each variable using a pipe with the summarize() function:

##### maybe clean up with across()

ny_noaa %>% 
  summarize(
    prop_na_id = mean(is.na(id)), # Gets me the proportion of NAs in each variable
    prop_na_date = mean(is.na(date)),
    prop_na_prcp = mean(is.na(prcp)),
    prop_na_snow = mean(is.na(snow)), 
    prop_na_snwd = mean(is.na(snwd)),
    prop_na_tmax = mean(is.na(tmax)),
    prop_na_tmin = mean(is.na(tmin))
  )

```

**Dataset Description:** The dataset (previously cleaned for our class by Prof. Goldsmith) is comprised of `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and the `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables. The variables contain information on the weather station ID (_id_; character type), date of observation (_date_; date variable), precipitation in tenths of millimeter (_prcp_; integer variable), millimeter of snowfall (_snow_; integer variable), millimeter of snow dept (_snwd_; integer variable), maximum temperature in tenths of degrees Celsius (_tmax_; character variable), and minimum temperature in tenths of degrees Celsius (_tmin_; character variable).

Regarding missing values (NAs), we see that there are none for our ID and Date variables; however, there is a considerable amount of missing data for each of the remaining 5 variables, with `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$prcp))*100, 2)`% of observations missing in _prcp_, `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$snow))*100, 2)`% of observations missing in _snow_, `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$snwd))*100, 2)`% of observations missing in _snwd_, `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax))*100, 2)`% of observations missing in _tmax_, and `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin))*100, 2)`% of observations missing in _tmin_. This is particularly concerning for the precipitation and maximum temperature variables since it represents about half of the observations.

### Cleaning The Data

After analyzing the extent of the NA issue, we can go ahead and do some data cleaning. We first construct new day, month, and year variables from our already existing _date_ variable using our reliable _mutate()_ function. Second, in order to convert our precipitation, temperature, and snowfall variables into reasonable units, we need to recognize that these variables are given in tenths of their units of measure. Therefore, we can just take advantage of the _mutate()_ pipe and do simple division by 10. We can leave our _snow_ variable as is since it is already in regular millimeters:

```{r weather_cleaning}

# The 'day()', 'month()', and 'year()' functions I learned last semester during one my classes using the lubridate package, which is part of tidyverse. Notice also that I had to convert my variables variables to numeric due to errors:

ny_noaa_cleaned =
  ny_noaa %>% 
  mutate(
    day = as.numeric(day(date)), # Creating my day, month, year variables
    month = as.numeric(month(date)),
    year = as.numeric(year(date)),
    prcp = as.numeric(prcp)/10,
    snwd = as.numeric(snwd)/10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax)/10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)/10
  )

# Checking the newly created variables:

# Checking the dates:

ny_noaa_cleaned %>% 
  select(day, month, year) %>% 
  head()

# From the output of this quick check, the code worked :)

# Now, checking the numerical variables:

ny_noaa_cleaned %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_prcp = mean(prcp, na.rm = TRUE), # Removing my NAs for quick check
    mean_snow = mean(snow, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_tmin = mean(tmin, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# The mean values appear in decent units, so our conversion also worked.

```

We can now proceed to assess which are the most commonly observed values for our snowfall variable. We can make use of the _count()_ function we have used in the past to get the counts of values in the _snow_ variable. Then, in a pipe, we can make use of the _arrange()_ function we learned in our data wrangling lecture to arrange our values in descending order:

```{r snowfall_common}

ny_noaa_cleaned %>% 
  count(snow) %>% 
  arrange(desc(n)) # Using 'desc' to get output in descending order rather than ascending

```

**ANSWER:** From the output, we can see that the most common value is 0 millimeters of snowfall, with `r ny_noaa_cleaned %>% filter(snow == 0) %>% nrow()` observations. This makes sense since snow does not fall for most days of the year in New York. We can see that the second most common value are our NAs, with `r ny_noaa_cleaned %>% filter(is.na(snow)) %>% nrow()` observations, which represent the weather stations that did not report any snowfall as a whole, so not even zeros. Moreover, we see that the third most common value when there is actual snowfall is 25 millimeters, with `r ny_noaa_cleaned %>% filter(snow == 25) %>% nrow()` observations, which is a relatively small amount of snow.

### Two-Panel Plot: Average Max. Temperature

After our initial cleaning and exploring, we can create a two-panel plot by making use of the _ggplot_ package, which is embedded withing the _tidyverse_. Since we are only asked to show the maximum temperatures for the months of July and January across different years, we can use the _filter()_ function along with out _group_by()_ function to group by different weather station as well as months and years. Moreover, to get our average maximum temperature, we can make use of _summarize()_ in the same fashion as we did above:

```{r two_panel_plot}

ny_noaa_cleaned %>% 
  filter(month %in% c(7, 1)) %>% # Recall our months are in number format
  mutate( # Making use of mutate like in HW2 assignment to relabel my months
    month = case_match(
      month,
      1 ~ "January", # Matching '1' to 'January'
      7 ~ "July"), # Matching '7' to 'July'
    ) %>% 
  group_by(year, month, id) %>% # Grouping by month, year, and ID
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
   geom_point(aes(color = id), alpha = .2) + # Following example from lecture
  geom_line(aes(color = id), alpha = .2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + # Had too many weather IDs
  labs(title = "Average Max. Temperature by Weather Station Across Years (January & July)", 
       x = "Year (1981-2010)",   # Adding labels like I did in HW1
       y = "Average Max. Temperature (°C)",
       caption = "Data from the 'p8105.datasets' package")

```
############ horizontal facet? ask office hours...

As we can see from the output, ggplot automatically removes the NA values for visualization purposes. Moreover, we can see that the plot shows a general (and expected) pattern where January is colder than July. We also see that most of the observations follow an apparent structure: they for conglomerate around 0°C for January, whereas they conglomerate around 28°C for July. There is some outlier variability, with a sudden drop on average max temperature around 1995 for January. There is not much variation for the July data except for a data point around 1988.

### Two-Panel Plot: Max. vs. Min Temperature

We can now proceed to make an additional two-panel plot using the maximum and minimum temperature values (variables _tmax_ and _tmin_, respectively) with the entirety of our data set. We can do this in a fashion similar like above, but we will now utilize the _hexbin_ package to create graphs other than a scatter plot for the minimum vs. maximum temperature plot. For the snowfall plot, since we are dealing with an univariate plot, we can create a density distribution:

```{r max_vs_min}

# Following a similar process like above plus what we learned in lecture, we can create two data frames for each of the panels:

# Min and max temperature plot (i):

ggp_maxnmin = # Following naming conventions from lecture
  ny_noaa_cleaned %>% # Note we don't need to modify our data in this one
  ggplot(
    aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature", 
       x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)", 
       y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
       fill = "Observation Count",
       caption = "Data from the 'p8105.datasets' package")
  
# Snowfall distribution plot (ii):

# Since we need to make sure that the distribution of snowfall has no values less than zero or greater than 100, we can make use of the 'filter' function. Moreover, we can make use of the 'fill' argument to make the distinctions by year:

ggp_snowdist =
  ny_noaa_cleaned %>% 
  filter(
    snow > 0, snow < 100
  ) %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = as.factor(year), y = snow, fill = as.factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = seq(1981, 2010, by = 4)) + # I Googled this command
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year", 
       x = "Year", 
       y = "Snowfall (mm)",
       caption = "Data from the 'p8105.datasets' package")

# Now, putting everything together:

ggp_maxnmin + ggp_snowdist

```

######## thoughts on boxplot???
######## ask about googling commands?

**Description:** From the output, we can see that the left panel--corresponding to the Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature--shows a positive correlation between the two variables. This makes sense since we expect temperatures to not differ too much in a single day. Moreover, we see that in the case of the right panel, where we restricted to show between 0-100 mm of snowfall, the medians and IQ ranges remained consistent across the years. However, we also see that the years 1998, 2006, and 2010 show multiple outliers.

## Problem 2: Accelerometer Data in the NHANES Study

Our problem utilizes accelerometer data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) research study.To start, we will load the data and proceed to tidy it. We must note that the data is in CSV format, so we need to use the _read_csv()_ function (part of tidyverse package) to import our file. From manual inspection, I saw that we needed to skip 4 rows in the demographic data CSV in order to get to our data.

Moreover, we use the _filter()_ function to only include participants who are 21 years of age or older, and can use _drop_na()_ in order to drop missing values for the demographic variables. Moreover, the demographic data CSV contained the numeric codes utilized for each variable, so I relabeled to give appropriate names using _case_match()_ like we did in Problem 1, and we convert to ordered factors:

```{r import_and_clean}

# Loading each data set individually:

accel_data =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/nhanes_accel.csv",
           na = c("","NA", ".") # We use this to make sure R understands these patterns as NA
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() # Cleaning names


covar_data =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/nhanes_covar.csv",
           na = c("","NA", "."),
           skip = 4, # Skipping first four rows
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() %>% # Cleaning names
  filter(
    age >= 21 #Only including people 21 and older
  ) %>% 
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) %>%  #Dropping observations with missing values
  mutate(
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school", # using exact names from CSV
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"),
    
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male", 
      2 ~ "Female")
    ) %>% 
  mutate( # Now we need to make factors and organize
    sex = as.factor(sex),
    education = factor(education, levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"))
  )


# Used these lines of code to continuously inspect my data frame as I was going about adding cleaning steps in my pipes:

head(accel_data, 5)
head(covar_data, 5)

```
####### left or innner joinn????


After we tidied our data, we can now proceed to merge it. For this, we will make use of the common _SEQN_ variable that is found in both data frames. From the data wrangling lectures, we know that we can use the _left_join()_ function to do this so that we can preserve the observations from the cleaned demographic data:

```{r merging_dfs}

nhanes_merged = 
  covar_data %>% #Starting from the cleaned demographic data
  left_join(accel_data, by = "seqn")

# Checking the new data frame:

head(nhanes_merged, 5)

# It worked!

```

### Producing Reader-Friendly Table

To create our table, we can make use of the _pivot_wider()_ function that we covered in our data wrangling lectures. We can use the _count()_ function we used in Problem 1 to obtain the counts of men and women in each education category. Then, as we saw in the EDA lecture, we use _knitr::kable()_ to make this reader-friendly:

```{r friendly_table}

nhanes_merged %>% 
  group_by(education, sex) %>% # Grouping by the variables we need
  summarize(
    n = n() # getting our counts
  ) %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  ) %>% 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Female", "Male")) #Looked up how to modify headers

```

**Table Description:** From the table, we can see that the individuals in our sample who have an education level corresponding to less than high school are evenly split between males and females, with `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Male") %>% nrow()` males and `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Female") %>% nrow()` females. However, males dominate in the high school equivalent level, with `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Male") %>% nrow()` males and `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Female") %>% nrow()` females. Lastly, once we reach upper levels of education, females take the lead in the more than high school category, with `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Male") %>% nrow()` males and `r nhanes_merged %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Female") %>% nrow()` females.

### Total Activity per Participant

From our cleaned data frame, we can now produce a new variable representing the total activity from each of the participants in the sample. Quick visual inspection of the accelerometer data reveals that it was collected by the minute. Therefore, we can make use of the _pivot_longer()_ function we covered in our data wrangling sessions and used in Homework 2. We also need to recall that, based on the article provided by Prof. Goldsmith, we use the unit _MIMS_, which stands for _Monitor-Independent Movement Summary unit (MIMS-unit)_, to refer to our values for each minute of a 24-hour day starting at midnight:

```{r total_activity}

total_act_df =
  nhanes_merged %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440, # Checked how many minutes are in a day to obtain this
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS" # Using the naming convention from the instructions and article
  ) %>% 
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) %>% # Grouping minute rows and keeping demographics
  summarize(total_act = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE) # Getting our total activity by summing day MIMS
  )
    
# We now quickly inspect the new data frame:

head(total_act_df, 5)

```

### Total Activity Across Age, Sex, and Education Groups

We successfully created our total activity variable and kept our demographic variables! We can now proceed to create our total activity vs. age graph while comparing the sexes and having separate panels for each education level. We will, of course, make use of ggplot for this:

```{r}

total_act_df %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = age, y = total_act, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = sex), alpha = 0.5) + # Grabbed from lecture example
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),) + # Googled how to center my title
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(title = "Total Activity Trend Across Ages (Subdivided by Sex and Education Level)", 
       x = "Age", 
       y = "Total 24-hour Activity (MIMS)",
       color = "Sex",
       caption = "Data publicly available from NHANES study.")

```

**Plot Description:** The graphs produced clearly demonstrate a negative correlation between total activity (in MIMS) and age, where people become more sedentary as they become older, irrespective of age, sex, or education level. Moreover, we see slight increases in activity after the age of 60, potentially due to post-retirement activities.

However, we can see that the decline in total activity is more pronounced for those with an education level less than high school, with female individuals in this group becoming more sedentary compared to males after the age of 40. Moreover, those with an education level more than high school show less pronounced decline in physical activity, gradually decreasing after the age of 50. It is also interesting to note that in both education levels for high school equivalent and more than high school, female individuals tend to be relatively more active compare to men.

### Activity Throughout the Day

In a similar way like how we created the data frame for total activity, we can now group our minutes by each participant to show the differences in activity in a single day. We will still make use of _ggplot_ to create our plot similarly like in the last section:

```{r in_a_days_life}

daily_act_df =
  nhanes_merged %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440, # Total minutes in a day
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min", # Removing the prefix
    values_to = "MIMS" # Using the naming convention from the instructions and article
  ) %>% 
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute)) %>%  # Converting to numeric
  group_by(sex, education, minute) %>% # Keeping the variables we need
  summarize(avg_MIMS = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE)) # Creating average MIMS activity for each minute
 

# Inspecting the data frame:

head(daily_act_df, 5)
  
# We can now create our plot in a similar fashion as before:
  
daily_act_df %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = minute, y = avg_MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = sex), alpha = 0.05) + # Grabbed from lecture example
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),) + # Centering my title
  facet_grid(. ~ education) + 
  labs(title = "Accelerometer Activity in 24 Hours (Subdivided by Sex and Education Level)", 
       x = "Minute in the Day", 
       y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
       color = "Sex",
       caption = "Data publicly available from NHANES study.")




```
######### should I keep geom_point or maybe move to geom_line?

**Plot Description:** The graphs produced clearly demonstrate a general trend: there is slight activity in the first minutes of the day (late night), which one may speculate it is due to not having reached deep sleep yet or just getting into bed. Then, approximately around the minute 400 (corresponding to the 6-7 AM time mark) all groups have a drastic increase in activity corresponding to the start of their day. This pattern persists irrespective of sex or education level. However, we can see that the group with education level less than high school has a higher average MIMS in the first hours of the day compared to the other education groups. Moreover, female individuals seem to have slightly more activity throughout the day compared to males in all education groups. It is also interesting to highlight that the those with ecucation more than high school have a plateau in their average activity for most of the day, potentially due to more sedentary jobs, compared to those with less than high school education.

## Problem 3: Citi Bike Data

For this problem, we are utilizing Citi Bike data for New York City. Just like we did in the last problem, we will start by importing, cleaning, and tidying the data. Just like in the previous problem, we see that the data is in CSV format, so we need to use the _read_csv()_ function again to import our file. Also like in the previous problem, we need to import each of the four provided files one by one.

Once imported, we can follow a process similar to what was done in Homework 2, where we used the _bind_rows()_ function to merge different files. However, we need to ensure we create a distinguishable identifier to ensure we know where the data is coming from. Considering that the only distinct difference between each set is the date, we can create variables for the year and month. I had to keep these as separate because we filter only be year in another step below (learned the hard way):

```{r importing_cleaning_bikes}

# Loading each data set individually and cleaning names:

jan20_citi =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv",
           na = c("","NA", ".") # We use this to make sure R understands these patterns as NA
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() # Cleaning names

jan24_citi =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv",
           na = c("","NA", ".") # We use this to make sure R understands these patterns as NA
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() # Cleaning names

jul20_citi =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv",
           na = c("","NA", ".") # We use this to make sure R understands these patterns as NA
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() # Cleaning names

jul24_citi =
  read_csv(file = "./HW3_Data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv",
           na = c("","NA", ".") # We use this to make sure R understands these patterns as NA
           ) %>% 
  janitor::clean_names() # Cleaning names

# Checking everything looks good:

head(jan20_citi, 5)
head(jul20_citi, 5)
head(jan24_citi, 5)
head(jul24_citi, 5)

# Looks good! Now we can mutate to add year and month variables.

jan20_citi =
  jan20_citi %>% 
  mutate(month = "January", year = 2020)

jul20_citi =
  jul20_citi %>% 
  mutate(month = "July", year = 2020)

jan24_citi =
  jan24_citi %>% 
  mutate(month = "January", year = 2024)

jul24_citi =
  jul24_citi %>% 
  mutate(month = "July", year = 2024)

# Now, we need to merge these four different data frames using 'bind_rows()'_

citi_merged = bind_rows(jan20_citi, jul20_citi, jan24_citi, jul24_citi)

#Checking:

head(citi_merged, 5)

# Voila! All good :)
  
```
####### can I use dollar signs for inline R?


**Data Set Description:** From our merge, we now have a data frame with `r nrow(citi_merged)` observations and `r ncol(citi_merged)` variables using data corresponding to 1% of the NYC rides in four months from two different years: January and July in 2020 and 2024. Moreover, the variables include a distinct ride ID (_ride_id_), the type of bike used (_rideable_type_), the day of the which the bike ride took place (_weekdays_), the duration of the ride in minutes (_duration_), the station from which the ride started (_start_station_name_), a binary variable to describe the rider as member or casual rider (_member_casual_), and our newly created month and year variables.

As some interesting facts, on average, bikes rides in this data set lasted `r round(mean(citi_merged$duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` minutes, and the day of the week with the most rides was `r citi_merged %>% count(weekdays, sort = TRUE) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(weekdays)`.

### Producing Reader-Friendly Table

Following the same strategy as in the last problem, we can make use of the _pivot_wider()_ function and then use _count()_ to obtain the total number of rides in each combination of year and month, separated by casual riders and CitiBike members. We use _knitr::kable()_ again to make this reader-friendly:

```{r friendly_bikes}

citi_merged %>% 
  group_by(month, year, member_casual) %>% # Grouping by the variables we need
  summarize(
    n = n(), # getting our counts
    .groups = "drop_last" # R told me to add to remove a message
  ) %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) %>% 
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Month", "Year", "Casual", "Member"))


```

####### how much should we be describing in general?


**Table Description:** From the table created, we see that the July months have a significantly higher number of bike rides compared to January of the same year. This is expected since the summer months are warmer and more people do outdoor activities. Moreover, we see there is an increase in both casual and member riders between 2020 and 2024, by about `r round(((nrow(filter(citi_merged, year == 2024, member_casual == "casual"))/nrow(filter(citi_merged, year == 2020, member_casual == "casual")))-1)*100, 2)`% in casual riders and `r round(((nrow(filter(citi_merged, year == 2024, member_casual == "member"))/nrow(filter(citi_merged, year == 2020, member_casual == "member")))-1)*100, 2)`% in member riders.

### Popular CitiBike Stations

Another interesting question: which were the most popular stations in New York City during July 2024? To answer this, we can use the same strategy as in Problem 1 to obtain a count of for each unique station and then using _arrange()_ to obtain the results in descending order. We can then use _knitr::kable()_ again to produce our table:

```{r}

citi_merged %>% 
  filter(month == "July", year == 2024) %>% # Filtering for July 2024 results
  group_by(start_station_name) %>% 
  count(start_station_name) %>% 
  drop_na() %>%  # Removing missing values
  arrange(desc(n)) %>% # Using 'desc' to get output in descending order rather than ascending
  head(5) # Getting the top five results

```

**Table Description:** From the table created, we see that the the most frequented stations to start rides from in July 2024 were, in this order: (1) Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers with `r citi_merged %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July", start_station_name == "Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers") %>% nrow()` rides, (2) University Pl & E 14 St with `r citi_merged %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July", start_station_name == "University Pl & E 14 St") %>% nrow()` rides, (3) W 21 St & 6 Ave with `r citi_merged %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July", start_station_name == "W 21 St & 6 Ave") %>% nrow()` rides, (4) West St & Chambers St with `r citi_merged %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July", start_station_name == "West St & Chambers St") %>% nrow()` rides, and (5) W 31 St & 7 Ave with `r citi_merged %>% filter(year == 2024, month == "July", start_station_name == "W 31 St & 7 Ave") %>% nrow()` rides.

### Visualizing CitiBike Data

Now that we have done sufficient data exploration, we can move into visualizing our data to investigate the effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration. We can use the _summarize()_ function in order to calculate the median duration, and then pipe and use _ggplot()_ to create our graph:

```{r citibike_viz}

# Using our merged CitiBike data set:

citi_merged %>% 
  mutate(
    weekdays = factor(  # Had to convert to factor because weekdays was not organized before
      weekdays,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday","Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      ))) %>% 
  group_by(month, year, weekdays) %>% # Grouping by the variables that we need
  summarize(
    median_dur = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% # Calculating the median duration
  ggplot(
    aes(x = weekdays, y = median_dur, color = month, group = month)) + #Added group for line geom
  geom_point(aes(color = month)) + # Grabbed from lecture example
  geom_line() + # Line instead of smooth since categoricaal variable
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),) + # Centering my title
  facet_grid(. ~ year) + 
  labs(title = "Effects of Temporal Variables on CitiBike\nRide Duration in New York City (2020 & 2024)", 
       x = "Days of the Week", 
       y = "Bike Ride Median Duration (minutes)",
       color = "Month",
       caption = "Data publicly available from CitiBike. Obtained through P8105 course site.")
  
```

**Figure Description:** From the generated figures, we can see that in both 2020, the month of January had a smaller median bike ride duration in comparison to July. This is sensical given the cold in the winter months, making it less tolerable to spend prolonged periods of time outdoors.
Moreover, we see that the median bike ride duration for either month was higher in 2020 compared to 2024, where July 2024 was particularly higher. This may have been due to the novelty and excitement around the service in 2020, as well as the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic which, after months of lock down, created an incentive for people to spend more time outside. The drop in the median values in 2024 may be due to increase in ride fares.

In terms of days of the week, we see that January 2020, July 2020, and July 2024 have increases in median bike ride duration for the weekend days. Interestingly, this is not the case for Sundays in July 2024. We can speculate that, in the colder months, people may avoid weekend bike rides since they have the possibility to stay in rather than attending work or social gatherings.

### Visualizing Ride Duration Distribution by 2024 Membership and Bike Type

We can create one last figure representing a plot for 2024 data, when electric bikes were more widely available compared to 2020. We can follow the same approach we have been using in previous sections.

For this question, since we are dealing with a categorical vs. contnuous variable, I originally thought to go for a box plot to get a better visualization of the effects of electric bikes in descriptive distribution metrics like median and IQ ranges. However, because of the diversity in observation values for duration, box plots were not the best. I then opted for a density plot instead to see the impact of month, membership, and bike type in the probability distribution of the duration, but it also did not have the best presentation. Finally, I saw a violin plot was the best-looking option and added an indicator for median since it is less sensitive to outliers:

```{r duration_membership_biketype}

# Using our merged CitiBike data set:

citi_merged %>% 
  filter(year == 2024) %>% # Filtering only for 2024 data
  mutate(
    rideable_type = case_match( # Using case_match to create better labels
      rideable_type,
      "classic_bike" ~ "Classic Bike", 
      "electric_bike" ~ "Electric Bike"),
    member_casual = case_match(
      member_casual,
      "casual" ~ "Casual", 
      "member" ~ "Member"),
    ) %>% 
  ggplot(
    aes(x = month, y = duration, fill = month)) + # Duration on 'x' since density plot
    geom_violin(alpha = .5) + 
  stat_summary(fun = "median", color = "red") + #Visualizing median
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) + # Centering my title
  facet_grid(member_casual ~ rideable_type) + 
  labs(title = "Effects of CitiBike Membership Status and\nBike Ride in New York City (2024)", 
       x = "Month (Year 2024)", 
       y = "Bike Ride Duration (Minutes)",
       fill = "Month",
       legend = "Month",
       caption = "Data obtained from CitiBike through P8105 course site.")
  
```

###### can I like Zoom into my data?

**Figure Description:** From the generated figures, we can see that, in the year 2024, most ride durations were mostly in the 0-50 minute range.
